newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK lawmakers to debate call for Wang Dan release.
newsitem.headline: HK lawmakers to debate call for Wang Dan release.

text.p: Hong Kong politicians geared up for a legislative debate on Wednesday on a motion that urges China to immediately set free jailed dissident Wang Dan.
The motion was registered earlier on Wednesday by Ho Chun-yan of the Democratic Party, the largest party in the Legislative Council.
Beijing has sidelined the party, a vocal critic of Chinese policies, from the power structures that it is crafting to run the territory after China takes over Hong Kong next year.
The debate appeared certain to spark an angry response from China, which rejects all criticism of its human rights record and its harsh punishment of dissenters, analysts said.
The Legislative Council meets late on Wednesday.

Wang, a former student leader involved in the 1989 democracy movement, was imprisoned for 11 years last week in Beijing on charges of plotting to overthrow the Chinese government, after he wrote articles critical of China's communist government.

Democratic Party leader, lawyer Martin Lee, said Wang's jailing was cause for alarm in free-wheeling Hong Kong, which reverts to China in 237 days after over 150 years as a British colony. China plans to scrap Legco and install an appointed "provisional legislature" excluding Lee's party next July 1.
"A new fully appointed legislature will pass repressive laws as directed by Beijing," Lee wrote in an article on Wednesday.

He said Hong Kong faced a situation like that when dictator Adolf Hitler came to power in Germany and changed the laws through his control of the legislature, forcing German judges to pass judgements that inflicted grave injustices.
"There is good reason to fear that history will be repeated in Hong Kong," his article in the South China Morning Post said.
"The demise of our elected legislature will mean China's definition of subversion will be applied through our courts," Lee wrote.

"Today I am free to write commentaries in this and other newspapers....It is a liberty my party members and I frequently exercise. But there is good reason to question whether I or anyone else will be able to exercise this freedom of expression after 1997," Lee wrote.
"As we debate the motion...I will think one thing: today, Wang Dan. Tomorrow, you and me."
